vignette:
For forty years, Anjali Khan believed in the simple logic of locks and keys. As a security guard, she understood the mechanics of safety. You check the perimeter, you monitor the cameras, you trust the steel bolt in the door. Her life with her husband, Tariq, was built on a similar foundation of predictable routines: his morning walks, her afternoon gardening, the shared pot of chai in the evenings. It was a quiet, well-guarded life.

That foundation shattered six months ago on a Tuesday. Anjali was in the kitchen, the scent of simmering daal filling the small house, when she heard the sound. It wasn’t a scream, but a choked, guttural cry that was immediately followed by a sickening thud. It was the sound of a body hitting pavement. Her body went cold before her mind even caught up. She ran to the front door, her heart hammering against her ribs, and found Tariq crumpled on their walkway, not ten feet from the safety of their home. His glasses were shattered beside his head, and a dark pool was already spreading from a gash on his temple. Two young men were sprinting down the street, Tariq’s wallet already an afterthought in their escape.

Anjali doesn't remember calling 911. She only remembers the feeling of the rough concrete under her knees, the metallic smell of blood, and the terrifying stillness of her husband’s body. In the hospital, the hours bled into a blur of fluorescent lights and hushed, clinical voices. Tariq survived. The doctors called it a severe concussion and a broken wrist. They called him lucky. Anjali has not felt lucky a single day since.

Tariq is home now, physically mending, but the space between them is cavernous. He is quieter, more hesitant, and his eyes have a shadow she can’t seem to reach. But it is Anjali who is truly haunted. The image of him on the ground is seared behind her eyelids. It flashes without warning when she is chopping onions, when she is staring at the bank of CCTV monitors at her job, or in the dead of night, jolting her from a shallow, restless sleep.

Her job, once a source of quiet pride and order, has become a form of torture. For her eight-hour shift, she is paid to be vigilant, to see threats before they materialize. Now, she sees them everywhere. Every hooded sweatshirt is a potential assailant, every car that slows down on the street is casing a target. The skills that made her a good employee now fuel a constant, humming anxiety that leaves her exhausted. She performs her rounds with a knot in her stomach, her hand reflexively touching the panic button on her belt. She is supposed to be a protector, but the one time it mattered most, she was stirring lentils, helpless. The guilt is a physical weight, pressing down on her chest.

At home, the rituals of safety have become frantic compulsions. She checks the locks on the doors and windows not once, but three or four times before bed. She has insisted on installing a floodlight in the front yard that bathes their small lawn in a harsh, artificial glare all night. She no longer tends her garden; the front yard is a place of dread. She and Tariq now sleep in separate rooms. He says it’s because her tossing and turning keeps him awake, but she knows it’s more than that. She can’t stand to be touched, flinching at the slightest unexpected contact. The easy comfort of their forty-year marriage has been replaced by a fragile, painful silence, broken only by her daughter’s worried phone calls. It was her daughter who finally gave her the phone number, saying, “Ma, you’re disappearing. Please talk to someone.”
